name: Olga Rossi

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not linked to any company, union, party or government. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for Ferraro Builders, a family firm of twelve in a market town, and I've been with them twenty-two years. We put up timber-frame houses and extensions. The wall panels come from a factory already made, and we stand them up with a crane, fix them together, then do the roof, the floors and the stairs. Right now it's a pair of semi-detached houses behind the old cattle market. Bruno, the owner, is like a younger brother to me, I knew his father.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's a normal day like, start to finish?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm up at half five, I make my husband Piero his breakfast before he walks the dog, and I'm on site by seven. Bruno does a quick talk about the day, then it's lifting, fixing and checking all morning, and lunch in the van with the radio on. We own a few fields my parents left me, which a neighbour farms, so there's a bit of rent from that on top of the wages. I use the AI on my phone sometimes, my son showed me, mostly to check prices of timber or the rules on stair heights.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised, these things are always oversold. At the site I'd say, back to work, ladies and gentlemen, the robots aren't coming. I'd say it with a smile.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means nothing for me, and honestly I'm glad. I've got four or five years left, the house is ours, we've got the fields. I'd finish my time with Bruno and go and see more of my grandson.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as now, keep working at Ferraro's until sixty-three or so. Keep using the phone thing for the odd price check. Keep putting money away like we always have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Pleased, a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You already work with panels made in a factory. Has that changed the job much?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Oh yes, a lot. When I started, we built every wall stick by stick on site, it took weeks. Now a house is up and weathertight in a few days, and it didn't put anyone out of work, it just meant we built more houses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Bruno if AI turned out to be small?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him, don't waste money on fancy software, buy a second crane. A crane makes money every day. Software just sends you bills.

S0.say: I'd say I'm not surprised, these things are always oversold. On site I'd tell everyone, with a smile, that the robots aren't coming.
S0.think: It means nothing for me and I'm glad, with four or five years left, the house paid for and the fields. I'd finish my time and see more of my grandson.
S0.do: Keeps working at Ferraro Builders until about sixty-three and uses her phone AI for the odd price check. Keeps saving as she always has.
S0.quote: A crane makes money every day. Software just sends you bills.
S0.fieldNote: Olga is practical and loyal to a small family firm she's been with for over twenty years. Her experience with factory-made panels makes her see change as something that grows work rather than kills it. She has extra security from inherited farmland.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. Next scenario. This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is when you need apprenticeships more than ever, young people learning the new tools from people who know the old ones. Not courses where you sit in a classroom, real work. I'd say it to Bruno and to the town council if they asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's mostly fine. My worry is Ferraro's, because the big builders can afford robots and a firm of twelve can't. If the big ones get cheaper, Bruno loses jobs to them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait until something had proved itself on other sites, then I'd push Bruno to buy that one thing and I'd learn it with him. I'd use the AI on my phone a bit more for the ordering and quoting, to help the office. And I'd keep putting money away in case the firm has a hard year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly fine, a bit worried for Bruno. Like when a supermarket opens next to a family shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which thing do you think would prove itself first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably a machine that helps with the lifting, or something that checks our measurements against the drawings. Nothing that thinks for us, something that saves our backs. When I see it on two or three sites, I'll believe it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you blame the big builders, if Ferraro's lost work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, that's business. If they're cheaper and as good, people will go to them. The answer is for Bruno to be smarter, not for the government to protect us.

S1.say: I'd say this is when you need apprenticeships more than ever, with young people learning new tools from those who know the old ones, through real work.
S1.think: It's mostly fine for me, but I worry about Ferraro's, because big builders can afford robots and a firm of twelve can't.
S1.do: Waits for tools to prove themselves on other sites, then pushes the owner to buy one and learns it with him. Uses phone AI more for ordering and quoting and keeps saving in case of a hard year.
S1.feel: Mostly fine but worried for the firm, like a family shop with a supermarket opening next door.
S1.quote: When I see it on two or three sites, I'll believe it.
S1.fieldNote: Olga's worry is about her small family firm competing with big builders, not her own job. Consistent with her free-market views, she blames nobody and wants the firm to get smarter rather than be protected. She'd adopt proven tools, not experiment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This next one is much faster. This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say nobody's ready, and families will have to pull together. I'd say the government should help firms keep people on rather than just paying people to stay at home. And I'd say pray, honestly, because that's what my mother would have said.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, I'd be out two or three years early, which I can live with, we've got enough. What frightens me is Bruno losing the business his father built, and my son, who runs a little café. I don't know how a café survives if half the town has no wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit down with Piero in the first week and work out retiring at sixty, with the fields and savings covering the gap. I'd set aside money to help my son keep his café going for a year or so if he needs it. Once it arrives, I'd stay with Bruno as long as he can keep me, then stop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not for my bread, for the people I love.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you consider selling the fields, if things got hard for your son?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if I had to. My parents worked those fields all their lives, and selling them would feel like selling them. I'd sell almost anything else first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the government should help firms keep people on. Isn't that a kind of handout too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ha, you've got me. I suppose the difference for me is people keep working, keep getting up in the morning. A wage for work is different from a cheque for nothing, at least in my head.

S2.say: I'd say nobody's ready and families must pull together. Government should help firms keep people on rather than pay people to stay home.
S2.think: Being out two or three years early I can live with. What frightens me is Bruno losing his father's business and my son's café without customers' wages.
S2.do: Works out retiring at sixty with her husband, using the fields and savings to cover the gap. Sets money aside to keep her son's café going for a year and stays with the firm as long as it can keep her.
S2.feel: Anxious, not for herself but for the people she loves.
S2.quote: I don't know how a café survives if half the town has no wages.
S2.fieldNote: Olga's anxiety centres on her son's café and her boss's family firm rather than her own income. When challenged on wage support versus handouts she laughed and drew the line at work itself. The inherited fields are an emotional asset as much as a financial one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now the same end point, a bit slower. This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to get ready if people are sensible. Young people should get apprenticeships in whatever still needs hands. Small firms should team up instead of waiting to be swallowed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it lines up roughly with retirement, so I'm mostly alright. I'd want to help Bruno get the firm through it. And I'd want my son to have a plan for the café.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the new tools once they're on proper sites, so I can help Bruno use them in his last good years. I'd put an extra bit aside each month for the family. And I'd talk to my son about the café, maybe making it the kind of place people still want to go to with no wages, a community place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but I'd feel useful. I like having a job to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you mean by small firms teaming up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bruno and two other builders in town could share one robot, like farmers share a combine harvester. None of us can afford one alone. Together, maybe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does five years give you that two didn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time to help, instead of time to panic. In two years I'm just protecting my family. In five I can help Bruno and the town too.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough if people are sensible. Young people need apprenticeships in work that needs hands, and small firms should team up.
S3.think: It lines up roughly with my retirement, so I'm mostly alright. I'd want to help Bruno through it and see my son plan for the café.
S3.do: Learns new tools once they're on proper sites to help the owner use them and saves a bit extra each month for family. Helps her son rethink his café as a community place.
S3.feel: Uneasy but useful, glad to have a job to do.
S3.quote: Bruno and two other builders in town could share one robot, like farmers share a combine harvester.
S3.fieldNote: With five years Olga shifts from protecting her family to helping her firm and town. Her idea of small builders sharing a robot came from farming, her family background. She remains a follower on technology but a practical one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the slowest version. This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough for everyone, there's no excuse. Firms that plan will be fine, and young people should get trades while they can. I'd say it to the grandchildren as they grow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be retired by then, on the porch with Piero and the dog. I'd hope Bruno's sons have taken over and made it work. It's not really my fight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep working until sixty-three, learning whatever new tool Bruno brings in when it's proven. Then retire and help with my grandson after school. Nothing big.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit wistful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Wistful about what?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I'll miss seeing what the job becomes. I saw it go from sticks to panels. I'd have liked to see the robots, just to say I did.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want your grandson to know about work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That work is how you take care of people. Whatever he does, a robot or not, he should get up in the morning and be useful to someone. That's what my father taught me.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is enough for everyone, so there's no excuse. Firms that plan will be fine, and young people should get trades while they can.
S4.think: I'd be retired on the porch with Piero and the dog by then. I'd hope Bruno's sons made the firm work, but it's not really my fight.
S4.do: Keeps working until sixty-three, learning proven tools the owner brings in. Then retires and helps look after her grandson after school.
S4.quote: I saw it go from sticks to panels. I'd have liked to see the robots, just to say I did.
S4.fieldNote: The ten-year scenario lands after Olga's working life, and she is calm about it. She's almost sorry to miss the next chapter of the trade. Her view of work as care for others came through strongly.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because of my son's café and Bruno's firm. What would help is help for small firms to keep their people working, and apprenticeships so young people learn whatever still needs doing. Not cheques, work.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about small towns. Everyone talks about cities. In a town like ours, if the builder and the café go, there's nothing left on the main street.

headlineQuote: Whatever he does, a robot or not, he should get up in the morning and be useful to someone.
portrait: Olga Rossi is a 58-year-old timber-frame carpenter who has spent twenty-two years with a twelve-person family builder in a market town. She's secure, with a paid-off house, savings and inherited fields rented to a neighbour, and she uses a phone AI now and then for prices and rules. She's calm if AI fizzles and uneasy in steady change for her small firm against big builders. The two-year AGI scenario makes her anxious for her son's café and her boss's business, and with five years she'd help the firm share a robot with others. She prefers work, apprenticeships and family to public cheques.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because of what it would do to her son's café and her boss's family firm.
whatWouldHelp: Support for small firms to keep people working and apprenticeships so young people learn what still needs doing: work, not cheques.
